description: Catholic Social Teaching, Gaudium et Spes, justice and peace, and the work of CAFOD, Trocaire and Missio.
content_html:
Loving Our Neighbour: A Catholic Imperative

When Jesus was asked which commandment was the greatest, he gave two: love God and love your neighbour (Matthew 22:37–39). He illustrated the second with the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), making clear that “neighbour” crosses ethnic, religious and social boundaries. For Catholics, the duty to love the neighbour is not optional — it is integral to what it means to follow Christ. This duty is expressed locally (in parish communities), nationally (through Catholic charities and advocacy) and globally (through international agencies such as CAFOD, Trocaire and Missio).

Catholic Social Teaching (CST) is the name given to the set of principles and commitments that the Church has developed for applying the Gospel to the structures of society. It emerged in its modern form in 1891 with Pope Leo XIII’s letter on the condition of workers, and has been developed by every subsequent Pope. Its core principles include the dignity of the human person, the common good, solidarity, subsidiarity (decisions made at the lowest appropriate level), a preferential option for the poor, and care for creation.

Key Fact

Core principles of Catholic Social Teaching: (1) Dignity of the human person — every person is made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27); (2) The common good — the conditions of social life that allow all people to flourish; (3) Preferential option for the poor — the poor and vulnerable have a claim on society’s first resources; (4) Solidarity — we are all members of the human family, responsible for one another.

Gaudium et Spes: Joy and Hope

Gaudium et Spes (“Joy and Hope”) was one of the four constitutions produced by the Second Vatican Council (Vatican II), published in 1965. It is a landmark document that turned the Church’s gaze outward to the world. Paragraph 26 is specifically named in the GCSE specification: it describes the social order as something that must be built on truth, justice and love, and insists that the development of institutions serving the common good is a Christian duty. The document teaches that the joys and griefs of humanity are the joys and griefs of the Church too — the famous opening line is: “The joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the people of this age, especially those who are poor or in any way afflicted, these too are the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ.”

Before Vatican II, some Catholics understood the Church’s role as primarily sacramental and otherworldly. Gaudium et Spes explicitly rejected this separation: the Church is not above or outside the world but within it, sharing humanity’s struggles and called to transform unjust social structures. This commitment to engaging with the world on questions of poverty, war, human dignity and economic justice remains central to Catholic identity today.

Justice, Peace and Reconciliation

Catholic teaching on justice holds that justice is not merely a legal concept but a moral one rooted in the equal dignity of all human beings. The Catholic Bishops of England and Wales have consistently called for a “just wage” for workers, fair housing, and the protection of asylum seekers — all flowing from the Church’s Social Teaching. The Prophet Amos’s demand “let justice roll on like a river” (Amos 5:24) is often quoted in Catholic social action contexts.

Peace in Catholic teaching is not merely the absence of war but the fruit of justice (a phrase from the Latin opus iustitiae pax — the work of justice is peace). The Church calls Catholics to be peacemakers — echoing the Beatitude “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Reconciliation — the restoration of broken relationships between individuals, communities and nations — is understood as a practical expression of the Gospel command to love one’s enemy (Matthew 5:44).

CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) is the overseas development and relief agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales. Founded in 1962, it works in more than forty countries, responding to humanitarian crises and supporting long-term development. CAFOD’s work is grounded explicitly in Catholic Social Teaching: its campaigns address climate justice, food security, fair trade and the rights of workers. Each year CAFOD’s fast-day fundraiser engages millions of Catholics in England and Wales in practical solidarity with the world’s poorest communities.

Trocaire is the overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in Ireland (the name means “mercy” in Irish). Like CAFOD, it works to address structural poverty and injustice rather than simply providing emergency relief. Missio is the pontifical mission society of the Catholic Church, supporting the Church’s evangelising work (spreading the faith) alongside practical support for education and healthcare in mission territories. Together these three agencies represent the global reach of Catholic social action: local parish fundraising connects directly to international justice work.

The Gospel Call to Global Solidarity

The Catholic commitment to global solidarity is anchored in the parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:31–46), in which Jesus identifies himself with the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” For Catholics, serving the poor is not a supplement to faith but an expression of it. Pope Francis’s description of a “Church of the poor” draws directly on this tradition.

At a parish level in Britain today, Catholic Social Teaching shapes a wide range of activities: parish food banks, collections for CAFOD, campaigns against human trafficking (supported by groups like CSAN — Catholic Social Action Network), and parish twinning with communities in the developing world. The GCSE specification names specific agencies — CAFOD, Trocaire, Missio — because they are the institutional expression of this teaching, translating theological principles into concrete action for millions of the world’s poorest people.

Secular humanist approaches to global justice share some goals with Catholic Social Teaching — reducing poverty, promoting equality, protecting human rights — but ground them differently. Secular humanists appeal to human reason, the shared humanity of all people, and to frameworks such as the UN Declaration of Human Rights (1948) rather than to scripture or Church authority. They may argue that poverty relief and justice work are more effective when separated from religious motivations and missionary agendas.

Some critics argue that Missio, because it combines charitable work with evangelisation (spreading the Catholic faith), has a complex relationship with the communities it serves: development and conversion can become entangled in ways that complicate the purely humanitarian dimension. Catholic Social Teaching responds that authentic human development includes the spiritual dimension — it is not possible to fully serve a person while ignoring their soul. This tension is a useful contrasting perspective in a 12-mark Evaluate question.

Key Fact

CAFOD (England and Wales): overseas development and relief, grounded in CST; over forty countries. Trocaire (Ireland): poverty and injustice; the name means ‘mercy’ in Irish. Missio: pontifical mission society; supports evangelisation, education and healthcare in mission territories. All three translate the Gospel call to “love your neighbour” (Matthew 22:39) into global structural action.
exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on Catholic Social Teaching or the work of a named agency, cite at least one source. Strong choices: Matthew 22:39 (love your neighbour), Matthew 25:40 (whatever you did for the least), Gaudium et Spes paragraph 26 (the social order must be built on truth, justice and love), or Genesis 1:27 (imago Dei — the foundation of human dignity). Name the source AND explain how it supports the reason — a bare quotation earns fewer marks than a quotation plus development.

For the 12-mark Evaluate on Catholic Social Teaching (e.g. “The Catholic Church does more good through its social action than through its worship”), arguments FOR will use the work of CAFOD, Trocaire, Missio, and Matthew 25; arguments AGAINST will emphasise that the Mass and the sacraments are the ‘source and summit’ of Catholic life and that social action flows from worship. A non-religious view might argue secular charities do equivalent or better work without a religious mission. Your JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION must state which side is stronger and WHY.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Catholic Social Teaching (CST) applies Gospel values to the structures of society, with core principles including human dignity (imago Dei), the common good, solidarity and a preferential option for the poor. Gaudium et Spes (Vatican II, 1965) is the foundational modern document, declaring that the Church shares the joys and griefs of humanity and is committed to justice and peace in the world.
  • Justice and peace in Catholic teaching are not abstract ideals but practical imperatives: justice is the fair distribution of goods and rights required by human dignity; peace is the fruit of justice. Catholics are called to be peacemakers (Matthew 5:9) and to serve the poorest (Matthew 25:40) as an expression of their faith.
  • CAFOD (England and Wales), Trocaire (Ireland) and Missio (pontifical mission society) are the main institutional expressions of Catholic global social action. Each translates the Gospel command to “love your neighbour” (Matthew 22:39) into concrete development, relief and evangelisation work in the world’s poorest communities.

practice_questions.text:
Which Second Vatican Council document (1965) named in the GCSE specification describes the Church's commitment to the common good and the social order built on truth, justice and love?
A) Humanae Vitae
B) Laudato Si'
C) Gaudium et Spes
D) Lumen Gentium
Name the overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks: CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Catholic Social Teaching influences the work of CAFOD or a similar Catholic agency.
For each way, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- CAFOD's work is grounded in the CST principle of the preferential option for the poor — this means it prioritises the world's most vulnerable communities, because Catholic teaching holds that the poor have a special claim on the resources and attention of the Church and society.
- The CST principle of solidarity — that all people are members of one human family — is expressed in CAFOD's global reach: a parish in Birmingham raising money for a community in Sudan is a practical expression of the conviction that poverty anywhere is the concern of all people.
- Gaudium et Spes paragraph 26 grounds the work: the social order must be built on truth, justice and love, not just on charity — CAFOD therefore works on structural issues like trade justice and climate policy, not just emergency relief.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the command to 'love your neighbour' is important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons; named source integrated (e.g. Matthew 22:37-39, Matthew 25:40, Luke 10:25-37, Gaudium et Spes 26); both reasons clearly linked to significance for Catholic life and action.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate; source cited but not fully developed.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic relevant point; no source.

Acceptable points include:
- Jesus himself names love of neighbour as the second greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-39), making it inseparable from love of God; for Catholics, this means that a devout Catholic cannot ignore the suffering of others — service to the poor is service to God.
- The parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:40) makes the command concrete: 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me'; this means helping the poor, the hungry and the stranger is not optional charity but a direct encounter with Christ himself.
- Gaudium et Spes paragraph 26 grounds the command in the social order: the Church is committed to building a world in which the dignity of every person is respected, requiring Catholics to work not only for individual acts of charity but for structural justice.

practice_questions.text:
'The Catholic Church does more good in the world through its social action (like CAFOD) than through its worship.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; social action vs worship comparison developed accurately; Catholic teaching on the Eucharist as 'source and summit'; work of CAFOD/Trocaire/Missio cited; Matthew 25 and Matthew 22 used; non-religious view on secular vs religious charity; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source cited; conclusion reached.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- CAFOD works in over forty countries, responding to famine, conflict and climate disaster; Trocaire and Missio extend this reach globally; millions of people's lives are materially improved by the Church's social action in ways that cannot be attributed to worship.
- Matthew 25:40 makes social action the criterion of judgement: 'Whatever you did for the least of these...'; a non-believer cannot do this but a society can measure material improvements in wellbeing.
- Some would argue that the Church's global development work is its most compelling argument for its relevance in the modern world — it translates faith into action that crosses religious boundaries.

Arguments against:
- Catholic theology insists that the Eucharist is 'the source and summit of Christian life' — social action flows from and returns to worship; without the Mass, CAFOD would have no theological foundation for what it does.
- Secular charities such as Oxfam and Save the Children do comparable development work without a religious mandate; the distinctively Catholic contribution is not development work per se but the theological conviction that grounds it in the Gospel.
- Prayer, the sacraments and the worship life of the Church are the means by which Catholics receive the grace to sustain their social action; without spiritual nourishment, the motivation for justice work would diminish.

Conclusion: Candidates may argue either side. A strong conclusion might acknowledge that for Catholic theology the distinction is false — worship and social action are inseparable, each nourishing the other; but if forced to choose, the candidate can argue that social action has more measurable global impact, or that worship is the deeper foundation without which social action loses its distinctive character.

practice_questions.text: A Catholic parish in Newcastle is organising its annual CAFOD Fast Day collection. Give two reasons why this is important for Catholics.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid point (up to 2 marks total).
Acceptable points include:
- It expresses practical solidarity with the world's poorest people, fulfilling the Gospel command to love the neighbour (Matthew 22:39).
- It connects local parish life to the global mission of the Church and its commitment to justice (Catholic Social Teaching).
- It expresses the preferential option for the poor — a core principle of CST — in a practical and accessible way.
- It gives Catholics a way to apply the parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:40) in their daily lives.

Trocaire is the overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in _____, and its name means 'mercy' in the native language.

right: Overseas development and relief agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales
Overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in Ireland — 'mercy'

flashcard_questions.a: A body of teaching applying Gospel values to the structures of society, addressing poverty, justice, workers' rights and the common good.
A key document of Vatican II (1965) describing the Church's commitment to justice, peace and the common good in the modern world.
The Catholic Agency for Overseas Development — the overseas development and relief agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the preferential option for the poor?
flashcard_questions.a: The CST principle that the poor and vulnerable have a special claim on the Church's and society's first resources and attention.

flashcard_questions.q: What is solidarity in Catholic Social Teaching?
flashcard_questions.a: The principle that all people are members of one human family, mutually responsible for one another across national and social boundaries.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Gospel verse makes helping the poor equivalent to serving Christ himself?
flashcard_questions.a: Matthew 25:40 — 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.'
The pontifical mission society supporting the Catholic Church's evangelisation and development work in mission territories worldwide.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'the work of justice is peace' (opus iustitiae pax) mean in Catholic teaching?
flashcard_questions.a: Peace is not merely the absence of war but the fruit of just social conditions — injustice causes conflict.

glossary_terms.definition: A body of teaching developed by the Catholic Church applying Gospel values to the structures of society, addressing poverty, justice, workers' rights and the common good.
A key document of the Second Vatican Council (1965), describing the Church's relationship with the modern world and its commitment to justice, peace and the common good.
The Catholic Agency for Overseas Development — the overseas development and relief agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales, working in over forty countries.
The overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in Ireland; the name means 'mercy' in Irish.
The pontifical mission society supporting the Catholic Church in mission territories worldwide, funding evangelisation, education and healthcare.
In Catholic Social Teaching, the fair and proper distribution of goods, rights and responsibilities in society, required as a consequence of human dignity.
People who work actively to end conflict, build trust between divided groups and restore relationships broken by injustice or violence.

hero_image_caption: Catholic Social Teaching calls Catholics to love their neighbour locally, nationally and globally — expressed through agencies like CAFOD, Trocaire and Missio.
